words.means: A tiny piece of a company that you can own.
words.example: If Disney was a pizza, one share is one small slice.

words.means: The money a company has left after it pays all its bills.
words.example: You sell lemonade for $10. The lemons cost $4. Your profit is $6.

words.means: A company's report card. It says how much profit it made.
words.example: Apple shares its earnings four times a year.

words.means: When a company does better than grown-ups guessed.
words.example: Grown-ups guessed $1. It made $2. It beat!

words.means: When a company does worse than grown-ups guessed.
words.example: Grown-ups guessed $2. It made $1. It missed.

words.means: The place where people buy and sell shares.
words.example: It's like a giant trading card swap, but for companies.

words.means: What someone will pay for one share right now.
words.example: If many people want a share, its price goes up.

words.means: Using money now so it might grow later.
words.example: Planting a seed so it can grow into a tree.

words.means: Keeping money safe so you can use it later.
words.example: Putting coins in a piggy bank.

words.means: Owning a little of many things instead of a lot of one.
words.example: Not putting all your eggs in one basket.

words.means: Lots of excited talk that might not be true.
words.example: "This will go to the moon!" is hype, not a fact.

words.means: How brave or worried people feel about buying shares.
words.example: Sunny means people feel brave. Cloudy means they feel worried.

company.means: A team of people who sell something to make money.
company.example: Nike is a company. It sells sneakers.

profit.means: The money left after a company pays its bills.
profit.example: You sell lemonade for $10. The lemons cost $4. You keep $6.

share.means: A tiny slice of a company that someone can own.
share.example: Cut a pizza into 4 slices. One slice is one share.

stock.means: A big market where people buy and sell shares.
stock.example: It is like a giant swap meet for slices of companies.

price.means: What someone will pay for one share right now.
price.example: When lots of kids want a card, it costs more.

report.means: A company tells everyone how much money it made. It does this 4 times a year.
report.example: Disney shares its report card in November.

guess.means: Before the report card, experts guess the profit.
guess.example: They guess $2. That is the number to beat.

beat.means: The company made more than the grown-ups guessed.
beat.example: They guessed $2. It made $3. It beat!

miss.means: The company made less than the grown-ups guessed.
miss.example: They guessed $2. It made $1. It missed.

mood.means: How brave or scared people feel about buying shares today.
mood.example: Sunny means brave. Stormy means scared.

saving.means: Keeping money safe so you can use it later.
saving.example: You put $10 in a jar at the bank. It stays safe.

investing.means: Using money to buy a slice of a company so it can grow.
investing.example: It can grow more than a jar, but it can go down too.

interest.means: A little extra money the bank pays you for keeping your money there.
interest.example: Keep $10 in the bank for a year. Get 20 cents extra.

dividend.means: A little of a company's profit, shared with each owner.
dividend.example: Own one slice. Get $1 when the company shares.

candle.means: A tiny picture of one day of a price.
candle.example: A green candle means the price ended higher that day.

wick.means: The thin line on a candle. It shows the highest and lowest price that day.
wick.example: A long wick means the price went far, then came back.

trend.means: The way a price is going over many days: up, down or sideways.
trend.example: Most days end higher, so the trend is up.

support.means: A low spot a price keeps bouncing up from.
support.example: The price fell to $20 three times and bounced each time.

resistance.means: A high spot a price keeps stopping at.
resistance.example: The price hit $50 twice and turned back down.

breakout.means: When a price pushes up through its ceiling.
breakout.example: The ceiling was $50. Now it is $55. Lots of breakouts fail, too.

pattern.means: A shape on a chart. It is a clue, not a promise.
pattern.example: Two hills in a row is a pattern. The next day can still surprise you.

volume.means: How many shares people traded in a day.
volume.example: Report card days often have big volume.

average.means: A smooth line made from the middle of the last few prices.
average.example: It hides the wiggles, so the trend is easier to see.

quest.intro: Before we look at real companies, let's run our own! Help me run a lemonade stand.

company.title: Run a company
company.ask: Tap the cup to sell lemonade. Each cup sells for $1. Sell 10 cups!
company.done: You sold $10 of lemonade. The lemons cost $4. So you have $6 left. That is your profit! Your stand is a company: a team that sells something.

shares.title: Cut it into shares
shares.ask: You want a bigger stand, but you need money. Cut your stand into 4 slices. Tap a friend to sell them a slice for $5.
shares.done: Each slice is called a share. Your friends own a share of your stand now! You got $15 for a bigger stand. Real companies do this too.

price.title: Watch the price move
price.ask: Now lots of kids want a slice of your stand! Tap the buttons to see what happens to the price.
price.up: Make the price go up to $8.
price.down: Now make it go down to $4.
price.done: More buyers made the price go up. More sellers made it go down. That is how prices move every day!

report.title: Report card day
report.ask: It's time for your stand's report card! Grown-ups guessed your profit would be $6. Will you beat it or miss it?
report.result: Your stand made $7 of profit. That's more than $6, so it BEAT!
report.done: Real companies like Disney and Apple share a report card 4 times a year. Now you can guess theirs!

quest.finish: You did it! You know what a company, a share, a price and a report card are. You earned the Lemonade Boss badge!

CHAPTERS.title: Luna's Lemonade Stand
CHAPTERS.blurb: What a company, a share and a price are.

CHAPTERS.title: Save or Grow?
CHAPTERS.blurb: A savings jar or a money tree. When do you pick each?

CHAPTERS.title: Your Slice Pays You
CHAPTERS.blurb: Some companies share their profit with owners.

DIV.intro: Remember how Bear, Bunny and Frog each own a slice of your stand? When the stand makes a profit, it can share some with them!

payout.title: Pay the owners
payout.ask: Your stand made $8 of profit. It keeps $4 to grow. The other $4 goes to the owners: $1 for each slice. Tap each owner to hand out a coin!
payout.done: Every owner got $1, even you! A company can share its profit like this. That is a dividend.
payout.remember: A dividend is a bit of the profit. Each owner gets some.

snowball.title: Spend or replant?
snowball.ask: You own 4 slices, so you get $4 each season. You can spend it, or replant it to buy more slices. Which ends up with more slices? Guess, then tap!
snowball.done: Spending was fun, and that's OK! But replanting bought more slices. More slices pay more coins. It's like a snowball. It gets bigger as it rolls.
snowball.remember: Replanting dividends buys more slices, and more slices pay more.

real.title: Real companies
real.ask: Do these real companies pay dividends? Guess for each one, then flip the card!
real.yes: gives owners a bit of its profit, a few times a year.
real.no: puts its money back in to grow.
real.done: Some companies share profit with owners. Others put it all back into growing. Both are normal!
real.remember: Some companies pay dividends. Some use all their money to grow.

check.title: Quick check
check.done: Chapter done! You know what a dividend is.

DIV.finish: You are a Dividend Detective! Some companies share their profit with owners. Replant it, and it can grow.

DIV_CHECK.why: A dividend is a bit of profit. The company shares it with the people who own its shares.

DIV_CHECK.q: If you replant your dividends, you get…
DIV_CHECK.why: Replanting buys more slices, and more slices pay you more next time.

SAVE.intro: You made $10 at your lemonade stand. Nice! Now what? You can keep it safe, or help it grow. Let's try both.

jar.title: The savings jar
jar.ask: Put your $10 in a savings jar at the bank. The bank pays you a little extra each year to keep it there. Tap to make a year go by!
jar.done: Your money grew a tiny bit every year. It never went down. That's saving: safe and slow. The extra the bank pays you is called interest.
jar.remember: Saving is safe. It grows slowly, and it does not go down.

tree.title: The money tree
tree.ask: Now plant $10 as a money tree. That means you buy a slice of a company. Tap to make 10 years go by. Watch both lines!
tree.downYear: Oh no! A bad year. The tree lost some leaves. Don't worry. Wait and see.
tree.upYear: A good year! The tree grew.
tree.done: Some years the tree went down. But after 10 years it grew much more than the jar! That's investing: it can grow more, but it can go down too. It needs time.
tree.remember: Investing can grow more over many years. But it can go down too, so it needs time.

choose.title: Jar or tree?
choose.ask: Here's the secret: pick by WHEN you need the money. Need it soon? Use the jar. Need it in many years? Plant a tree. Sort each card!
choose.done: You sorted them all! Money for soon goes in the jar. Money for a long time from now can grow in a tree.
choose.remember: Soon means save. Far away means you can invest.

check.title: Quick check
check.done: Chapter done! Now you know when to save and when to grow.

SAVE.finish: You are a Smart Saver! You know that saving is safe and slow, and investing can grow more but needs time.

SAVE_CHECK.q: Which one can go DOWN some years?
SAVE_CHECK.why: An investment can go down in a bad year. Savings in the bank do not.

SAVE_CHECK.q: You need money for a game next week. Where should it be?
SAVE_CHECK.why: Next week is soon. Keep money you need soon in the jar.

SORT_ITEMS.why: Next week is soon. The tree might have a bad week, so keep it in the jar.
10 years is a long time. A tree has time to grow, even after bad years.

SORT_ITEMS.text: A birthday gift for Mom this month
SORT_ITEMS.why: This month is very soon. Keep it safe in the jar.
That's many years away. Lots of time for a tree to grow.
Next summer is not very far. The jar keeps it safe until then.

units.blurb: What money is, and how to plan it.

units.blurb: Spread out, be patient, check facts.

steps.text: Long ago, people traded things. A cow for some bread!
That was hard. What if the baker did not want a cow?
So people made money. Everyone agrees it is worth something.

steps.q: Why did people make money?
steps.why: Money makes trading easy, because everyone takes it.

steps.text: Grown-ups earn money by doing work. A cook cooks. A nurse helps sick people.
Kids can earn too! You can sell lemonade or help a neighbor.
Earning takes time and work. That is why money matters.

steps.q: How do most grown-ups get money?
steps.why: Most grown-ups earn money by doing a job.

steps.text: A need is something you must have. Like food, a home and clothes.
A want is something nice to have. Like a new game or candy.

steps.q: Is it a need or a want?
steps.why: Needs come first. Wants come next, if there is money left.

steps.text: A budget is a plan for your money. You plan before you spend.
Try three jars: Spend, Save and Share. Put some money in each one.
When you see something fun, check your Spend jar first.

steps.q: A budget is…
steps.why: A budget is a plan. It helps you choose before you spend.

steps.text: A company is a team of people. They work together to sell something.
Some sell things you can hold, like shoes or toys. Some sell things you use, like games or videos.
When people buy what it sells, the company gets money. If it gets more than it spends, the extra is profit.

steps.q: What does a company do?
steps.why: A company sells things or services to people.

steps.q: Profit is…
options: Money left after paying the bills
All the money a company spends
steps.why: Profit is the money left after the bills are paid.

steps.text: Money in is all the money a company gets from selling things.
Money out is what it pays for. Workers, rent and supplies.
Money in minus money out is profit. If money out is bigger, that is a loss.

steps.q: A shop sells $20 of cookies. The flour cost $5. What is the profit?
steps.why: $20 take away $5 is $15.

steps.text: A lemonade stand can grow into a lemonade shop.
To grow, it needs money for a bigger shop and more workers.
One way to get that money is to sell shares of the company.

steps.q: Why might a company sell shares?
steps.why: Selling shares brings in money the company can use to grow.

steps.text: Think of a big company like a pizza cut into lots and lots of slices.
Each slice is called a share. If you own a share, you own a tiny piece of that company.
People buy and sell shares in a place called the stock market. Grown-ups need a special account to do it.

steps.q: If you own a share of a company, you own…
steps.why: A share is a tiny slice of the company. Like one slice of a pizza.

steps.q: Where do people buy and sell shares?
steps.why: Shares are bought and sold on the stock market.

steps.text: If you own a share, you are a part owner of the company.
Owners can vote on some big choices. One share is one vote.
If the company does well, your share can be worth more.

steps.q: Owning one share of Nike makes you…
options: A tiny part owner of Nike
steps.why: One share makes you a tiny part owner. Lots of other people own parts too.

steps.text: The stock market is a big place where people buy and sell shares.
Today it is mostly on computers. It opens in the morning and closes in the afternoon.
In New York, a bell rings to start the day and to end it!

steps.q: What do people trade on the stock market?
steps.why: The stock market is where shares are traded.

lessons.title: Why do prices go up and down?

steps.text: The price of a share is what someone will pay for it right now.
When lots of people want to buy, the price goes up. When lots want to sell, it goes down.
It is a bit like trading cards. When everyone wants a card, people will give more for it.
Prices move every day. Small ups and downs are normal.

steps.q: If lots of people want to buy a share, the price…
steps.why: More buyers than sellers pushes the price up.

steps.q: Is it normal for prices to move a little every day?
steps.why: Prices wiggle every day. That is normal.

steps.text: Each company has a short nickname. It is called a ticker.
Apple is AAPL. Disney is DIS. Coca-Cola is KO.
Grown-ups use tickers to find a company fast.

steps.q: What is DIS?
steps.why: DIS is Disney's short nickname on the stock market.

steps.text: You get a report card from school. Companies get one too!
Four times a year, each company tells everyone how it did. Grown-ups call this an earnings report.
It says how much money came in, and how much profit the company made.
Metaphases shows when each company will share its report card. We draw the time as a moon.

steps.q: How many times a year does a company share its report card?
steps.why: Companies report four times a year, once every three months.

steps.q: What do grown-ups call a company's report card?
steps.why: It is called an earnings report.

steps.text: Before a report card, experts guess the profit.
They put all the guesses together and find the middle. That is the number to beat.
Then everyone waits to see what really happened.

steps.q: What are the experts guessing?
steps.why: They guess the profit, so we can see if the company beats it.

steps.text: Before a report card comes out, grown-ups make a guess. They guess how much profit the company will make.
If the company makes more than the guess, it beat. If it makes less, it missed.
Sometimes a company beats and the price still goes down. People may have hoped for even more!

steps.q: Grown-ups guessed $2. The company made $3. Did it beat or miss?
steps.why: $3 is more than the $2 guess, so it beat.

steps.q: Can a price go down even when a company beats?
steps.why: Yes! People may have hoped for even more good news.

lessons.title: Why prices jump on report day

steps.text: On report card day, prices can jump up or fall down fast.
That is because people learn lots of new facts all at once.
People also hear what the company thinks comes next.

steps.q: Why can a price jump on report card day?
options: People learn new facts all at once
steps.why: New facts arrive all at once, so people change their minds fast.

steps.text: Saving is keeping your money safe, like in a piggy bank. It stays the same.
Investing is using money to buy things like shares. It can grow, but it can also shrink.
Grown-ups often do both. They save money they need soon. They invest money they will not need for a long time.

steps.q: Money in a piggy bank…
steps.why: Saved money stays the same. It does not grow or shrink.

steps.q: Investing can make money…
steps.why: Investing can go up or down. That is the risk.

steps.text: A bank keeps your money safe. It even pays you a little to keep it there.
That little extra is called interest. Put in $100, and a year later you may have $102.
Interest is slow, but it is safe.

steps.q: Interest is…
options: A little extra money the bank pays you
steps.why: It is the small extra the bank adds to your money.

steps.text: Roll a snowball and it picks up more snow. It gets bigger faster and faster.
Money can do that too. The money you grow can grow more money.
That is why starting early helps. Time makes the snowball big.

steps.q: Why does starting early help?
options: More time for the snowball to grow
steps.why: More years means more time for growth to pile up.

steps.text: Risk means things might not go the way you hope.
A savings jar has low risk. It will not grow much, but it will not shrink.
Investing has more risk. It can grow more, but some years it goes down.

steps.q: Low risk or high risk?

items.text: All your money in one new company
A stock a video says will go to the moon

steps.why: Safe places grow slowly. Big promises can go up or down a lot.

steps.text: Need the money soon? Save it. Then it will be there when you need it.
Will you not need it for many years? Investing gives it time to grow.

steps.q: Save it or invest it?

items.text: A gift for mom this month

steps.why: Soon means save. A long time means it can be invested.

steps.text: Some companies share part of their profit with their owners. That is a dividend.
If you own a share, you might get a little money every few months.
Coca-Cola and McDonald's pay them. Some do not.

steps.q: A dividend is…
options: Profit a company shares with its owners
steps.why: It is a bit of the profit. The owners get it.

steps.text: Some companies keep all their profit to grow faster.
They build new things, hire workers and open new stores.
Owners hope the company grows. Then their shares may be worth more later.

steps.q: Why might a company skip dividends?
options: To use the money to grow
steps.why: Some companies use all their profit to grow.

steps.text: When you get a dividend, you can spend it. Or you can use it to buy more shares.
Buying more shares is like adding snow to your snowball.
Over many years, that can grow a lot.

steps.q: Using dividends to buy more shares is like…
steps.why: More shares can pay you more. So the snowball grows.

lessons.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket

steps.text: Imagine you carry all your eggs in one basket. If you trip, they all break!
If you split them into many baskets, one trip only breaks a few.
Money works the same way. Owning a little of many companies is safer than a lot of one.
Grown-ups call this spreading out. You can try it in your Piggy Bank.

steps.q: Why split your eggs into many baskets?
options: So one trip doesn't break them all
steps.why: If one basket falls, the others are still safe.

steps.q: Which is safer?
options: All your money in one company
steps.why: Spreading out means one bad day hurts less.

steps.text: The moon takes about a month to go from new moon to full moon. It does not rush.
Good companies can grow over many years. Some days their price goes down. Some days it goes up.
People who wait a long time often do better than people who buy and sell every day.

steps.q: Good investing is usually…
steps.why: Waiting a long time usually works best.

steps.q: If a price goes down for one day, should you panic?
steps.why: Prices go up and down. One bad day is normal.

steps.text: Sometimes a video says a stock will go to the moon. That is called hype.
Hype is exciting. But the person in the video might be trying to sell, or might just be wrong.
Facts are things you can check, like how much profit a company made.
Before you believe a video, ask: What are the facts? Who is telling me this? Why?

steps.q: A video says "this stock will go to the moon!" That is…
steps.why: It's an exciting guess, not a fact you can check.

steps.q: What should you do before believing a video?
steps.why: Always check the facts, and ask a grown-up.

steps.text: If someone promises lots of money, fast and for sure, that is a red flag.
Real investing has ups and downs. Nobody can promise it only goes up.
If it feels too good to be true, stop and ask a grown-up.

steps.q: Someone says "Double your money by Friday, for sure!" What do you do?
steps.why: Big promises that are for sure are a red flag. Ask a grown-up.

steps.text: A candle is a tiny picture of one day of a price.
The fat part is the body. It shows where the price started and where it ended.
Green means the price ended higher than it started. Red means it ended lower.

steps.q: A candle is green. What happened that day?
steps.why: Green means it ended higher than it started.

steps.text: The thin lines on the top and bottom are called wicks.
The top of the wick is the highest price that day. The bottom is the lowest.
A long wick means the price went far, then came back.

steps.q: What does the top of the wick show?
steps.why: The top of the wick is the highest the price got that day.

steps.q: Green or red candle?
steps.why: Ended higher is green. Ended lower is red.

steps.text: Some days, buyers and sellers pull hard both ways, like a game of tug-of-war.
The price goes way up and way down, but ends near where it started.
That candle has a tiny body and long wicks on top and bottom.

steps.q: A candle has a tiny body and long wicks. What kind of day was it?
steps.why: Long wicks and a tiny body mean the price swung both ways.

steps.text: A trend is the way a price is going over many days.
If most days end higher, the trend goes up.
If most days end lower, the trend goes down.
Prices wiggle every day. Look at the big picture, not one day.

steps.q: A price wiggles but keeps climbing for a month. The trend is…
steps.why: It keeps climbing, so the trend is up, even with wiggles.

steps.text: Sometimes a price goes up, then down, then up again, but stays in the same place.
That is a sideways trend. It is like walking on flat ground.

steps.q: A price starts at $10. After a month of wiggles it is still $10. The trend is…
steps.why: It ended where it started, so it went sideways.

steps.text: A trend shows what already happened. It does not promise what comes next.

steps.q: Does an up trend promise the price will keep going up?
steps.why: A trend can change any day. It is a clue, not a promise.

steps.text: One day can look scary. Ten days can tell a calmer story.
Zoom out to see more days. The trend is easier to spot.
People who invest for years look at years, not days.

steps.q: One red day in a month of green days. What is the trend?
steps.why: One red day does not change a month of going up.

steps.text: Sometimes a price keeps falling to the same low spot, then bounces. That spot is the floor.
Sometimes a price keeps stopping at the same high spot. That spot is the ceiling.
Grown-ups call the floor support. They call the ceiling resistance.

steps.q: A price keeps bouncing up from $20. What is $20?
steps.why: A spot it keeps bouncing up from is the floor.

steps.text: When a price pushes up through its ceiling, that is a breakout.
When a price falls through its floor, that is a breakdown.
Lots of breakouts fail. The price can fall right back. That is normal!

steps.q: The ceiling was $50. Now the price is $55. What happened?
steps.why: It pushed up through the ceiling. That is a breakout.

steps.text: Shapes on a chart are clues. They show what happened before.
A clue is not a promise. News and surprises can change the price fast.
People who know a lot still guess wrong. That is normal.

steps.q: A chart shows a shape you know. What does it mean?
options: It is a clue, not a promise
steps.why: A shape is only a clue. Nobody knows for sure what comes next.

steps.q: Who knows for sure what a price will do next?
steps.why: Nobody can know for sure. Not even experts.

steps.text: Volume means how many shares people traded in a day.
A busy day has lots of trading. A quiet day has a little.
Report card days are often busy. Lots of people react to the news.

steps.q: What does volume tell you?
steps.why: Volume counts how many shares changed hands.

steps.text: Prices zig and zag. That can make the trend hard to see.
A moving average takes the last few prices and finds the middle.
That makes a smooth line. It helps you see the trend.

steps.q: Why do people use a moving average?
options: To see the trend more easily
To make the price go up
steps.why: The smooth line hides the wiggles, so the trend is easier to see.

steps.text: On report card day, a price can jump up or drop down fast.
A beat can make a price jump. But not always!
Sometimes a company beats and the price still drops. People wanted even more.

steps.q: A company beat the guess. Will the price always go up?
steps.why: Not always. People may have wanted even more.

fkGrade.text: A share is a tiny piece of a company.
Consensus estimates incorporate analysts' expectations regarding quarterly profitability and operational efficiency.
Long ago, people traded things. A cow for some bread!
That was hard. What if the baker did not want a cow?
So people made money. Everyone agrees it is worth something.
Grown-ups earn money by doing work. A cook cooks. A nurse helps sick people.
Kids can earn too! You can sell lemonade or help a neighbor.
Earning takes time and work. That is why money matters.
A need is something you must have. Like food, a home and clothes.
A want is something nice to have. Like a new game or candy.
A budget is a plan for your money. You plan before you spend.
Try three jars: Spend, Save and Share. Put some money in each one.
When you see something fun, check your Spend jar first.
A company is a team of people. They work together to sell something.
Some sell things you can hold, like shoes or toys. Some sell things you use, like games or videos.
When people buy what it sells, the company gets money. If it gets more than it spends, the extra is profit.
Money in is all the money a company gets from selling things.
Money out is what it pays for. Workers, rent and supplies.
Money in minus money out is profit. If money out is bigger, that is a loss.
